rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds while minimizing the risk of non-elution. The retention window and critical pair resolutions will guide subsequent slope and temperature adjustments.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test a faster method while retaining the substantial resolution margin.
Shorten the gradient another grid step while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed. The current minimum resolution of 3.24 provides room to reduce elution time while preserving the maximum CRF.
Test the next shorter gradient with endpoints and temperature unchanged. The resolution trend suggests the critical early pair may remain above 1.5, giving a faster method at the maximum CRF.

The 4-minute gradient retains maximum CRF but has little resolution margin for further steepening. Raise temperature one step to test faster elution and its effect on the critical early pair, keeping injection 4 as the fully resolved fallback.

Higher temperature worsened the critical pair, so test a cooler, 2-minute gradient for improved selectivity at shorter run time. Lowering the endpoint to 0.80 moderates the gradient slope, followed by a strong-organic hold to elute the final compound.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce the gradient slope while retaining the 0.80 endpoint for prompt late-peak elution. Test whether this lifts the critical pair from R = 1.48 above 1.5 without sacrificing the shorter run.

Shift both gradient endpoints upward by 0.05, preserving the slope that achieved full resolution in injection 7. The stronger endpoint should accelerate the last peak; monitor whether the critical early pair retains R ≥ 1.5.

Shift both endpoints upward another step while preserving gradient slope and temperature. This should further accelerate the last peak while testing whether the early pair maintains its resolution margin.

Continue the successful upward shift of both endpoints at constant slope, now reaching the maximum final organic fraction. Test whether this shortens late-peak elution while preserving full resolution and CRF 1.000.

Raise only the starting organic fraction to narrow the gradient window and accelerate elution. Check the early pair carefully as it approaches the solvent front, retaining injection 10 as the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Increase the starting organic fraction one more step, since the previous increase improved minimum resolution while slightly shortening elution. Monitor compression of the early pair near the dead time.

Back off the starting fraction to 0.30, where full resolution was retained, and raise temperature one step to shorten elution. This tests whether the early pair’s R = 1.77 margin can accommodate the temperature increase.
Test one further temperature step to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The early pair may fall below 1.5; injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved method if that occurs.

Reduce the final organic fraction to moderate the slope and test whether full resolution can be recovered at 35 C. This explores the balance between early-pair resolution and late-peak hold time; injection 13 remains the fastest maximum-CRF method.

Lower the starting organic fraction to retain the early pair longer, where gradient selectivity may restore its resolution. The weak response to changing the endpoint alone suggests that early elution near the dead time is limiting separation at 35 C.

Return to 30 C, which preserved full resolution, and shift the successful injection 13 window downward by 0.05 at unchanged slope. This tests a maximum-CRF alternative with the early pair farther from the dead time and only a modest expected increase in late-peak retention.

Test the endpoint between injections 13 and 15 at the successful 30 C temperature. The shallower slope may improve the early-pair resolution margin relative to injection 13 while keeping late-peak elution close to the fastest fully resolved result.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a cooler alternative to injection 17 for greater resolution margin while keeping the early peaks farther from the dead time. Injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Test the cooler counterpart of injection 18 to increase the critical-pair resolution margin while maintaining rapid elution. This also completes a local endpoint–temperature comparison around injection 13, the fastest method achieving maximum CRF.
Maximum CRF is already secured; test one lower endpoint for additional early-pair resolution margin with a modest time tradeoff. Injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.
